From CAD to Rocket Hardware: Akkoyun Aerospace’s Carvera Story – Makera
— Yasin Akkoyun, Founder of Akkoyun Aerospace
From Model Aircraft to an Aerospace Company

After finishing school in 2025, he decided toward the end of that year to focus seriously on rocket technology. Those personal projects began evolving into Akkoyun Aerospace, an early-stage company in Germany with the long-term goal of developing orbital launch vehicles for small satellites and mission-specific payloads.
“For me, getting the Carvera wasn't just about buying another tool. It gave me the opportunity to learn an entirely new manufacturing process.”

One project Yasin is particularly proud of is the SRS VCTR-04, an electromechanical linear actuator designed to control the direction of the rocket engine. Now in its fourth major design iteration, it brings mechanical design, precision manufacturing, and control engineering together in a compact assembly.

“Having the Carvera in my workshop makes this approach possible because I can move between designing, manufacturing, and testing without having to organize a new manufacturing order for every iteration.”
Revised CAD design: separating the components enabled a simpler three-axis manufacturing process.

Some days are devoted to CAD and calculations. Others are spent manufacturing, and Yasin often designs in the morning and machines in the afternoon. Testing gets its own dedicated days. Alongside vehicle hardware, he makes the custom fixtures, test equipment parts, and supporting components that keep development moving.

The next major goal is the first flight of the VTVL demonstrator, bringing together systems he has been developing individually. That milestone is still ahead. The progress so far lies in the physical components, revised designs, and manufacturing experience that make the next stage possible.

The revised assembly gave each manufacturing process a clear job. The Carvera Air machined the aluminium sections, which the team then bonded into the printed bracket. CNC machining produced the metal parts, while 3D printing supplied the connecting geometry.

That four-hour period covered learning the software, redesigning the component and manufacturing it. The experience gave students a direct connection between a material limitation, a design decision and the parts they could actually make.

The team also cut carbon fibre spars on the Carvera Air. These parts sit deeper within the aircraft’s wing and fuselage connection areas, where they are less visible in a photograph of the complete aircraft. The machining footage documents that part of the manufacturing process.

Atelier3 is a film and TV production company focused on outdoor sports. Its crew shoots documentaries and branded films in conditions where there’s little time to reset equipment—and where every camera, lens, battery, and accessory has to be carried up and down the mountain.
Changing a camera from a tripod setup to a gimbal can take five minutes or more if it means removing cables and swapping plates. On a training day with only a handful of runs, those minutes matter.

“Being able to change from a tripod to a stabilizer to a handheld rig in thirty seconds” is the goal, he says. A custom plate lets the same camera move from tripod to gimbal without changing the plate underneath. Once the camera is balanced, the operator can make the switch with a quick release and a couple of adjustments.

Weight matters just as much. The team may carry two cameras, lenses, batteries, rigging, and a tripod—a load that can reach 30 kilograms. Atelier3 looks for ways to combine functions or remove even small amounts of weight from a pack or camera rig.

The K-3, a compact 16mm film camera, was a good candidate. In its original form, it had few mounting points, a single tripod hole, and a shutter button that was difficult to reach when the camera was on a gimbal. The operator also couldn’t easily monitor the image through the viewfinder in that configuration.
The machine itself quickly became part of the workshop routine.
